intro: Lansing's two old trees are both in East Lansing, on the Michigan State University campus about five kilometres east of downtown. The Resilient Oak on the Campus Oval gave up 347 annual rings after a 2016 storm, and its curator puts it at 375 to 400 years. In Beal Botanical Garden stands a dawn redwood planted in 1954, a species thought extinct until the 1940s, with a lightning arrestor of its own. Both are free to visit and stops on the campus tree tour.
meta_description: East Lansing's Resilient Oak, a white oak with 347 counted rings and a 375 to 400 year estimate, on the Michigan State University campus.
question_meta: The Lansing area's oldest mapped tree is the Resilient Oak in East Lansing, 347 rings counted, estimated at 375 to 400 years.
question_answer: The oldest tree we map around Lansing is the Resilient Oak, a White Oak (Quercus alba) on the Michigan State University campus in East Lansing. A section above the base showed 347 annual rings after a storm in 2016, and the campus arboretum's curator estimates the whole tree at 375 to 400 years.
question_context: It is a rare thing to have counted rings on a tree you can still go and see. The storm of 8 July 2016 blew the oak over, and a 20-foot section above the base gave up its rings. The curator's 375 to 400 allows for slow growth under shade. The university describes the tree as a survivor of the forest that covered this ground before 1855. It was topped about a century ago, an operation in the college's own 1915 history that left a metal cap, and it lost roots to a sidewalk. It was named in the autumn of 2017. What remains is a hollow trunk at the edge of the path, near Beaumont Tower, stop 8 on the campus tree tour, and reports from 2024 and 2025 say it keeps growing. Other old oaks stand around the Oval, and the tour suspects they are survivors too, but none has dated rings. A short walk west, in Beal Botanical Garden, the dawn redwood planted in 1954 is the first stop on the same tour. East Lansing lies about five kilometres east of downtown Lansing.

faq.q: How do we know the age of the Resilient Oak?
faq.a: After it blew over in 2016, a 20-foot section above the base showed 347 annual rings. The curator's estimate of 375 to 400 years allows for slow growth in shade.

faq.q: Is the Resilient Oak in Lansing or East Lansing?
faq.a: East Lansing, on the Michigan State University campus near Beaumont Tower, about five kilometres east of downtown Lansing.

faq.q: Why does the dawn redwood at Beal Garden have a lightning arrestor?
faq.a: Lightning struck it in the 1990s. An arrestor was fitted in October 2012, and in 2017 the university said more than 20 feet would come off the top because of decay from the lightning crack.

trees.name: The Resilient Oak

location.address: MSU Campus Oval near Beaumont Tower, East Lansing, MI 48824 (beside the sidewalk)
location.neighbourhood: Michigan State University campus, East Lansing

trees.story:
Somebody counted 347 rings in this oak, and that was only in a section above the base. On 8 July 2016 a storm blew the tree over on Michigan State University's campus in East Lansing, and the curators got what they rarely get with a living landmark, a look at its record. The 20-foot section gave them 347 annual rings. Because it grew slowly in shade, the curator of the campus arboretum estimates the whole tree at 375 to 400 years.

It is described as a survivor of the forest that covered this ground before 1855, and it has not had an easy time since. It was topped about a hundred years ago, an operation recorded in the college's own history of 1915, complete with a metal cap. A sidewalk took some of its roots. Then the storm.

The university named it the Resilient Oak in the autumn of 2017. What stands today is a hollow trunk at the edge of the path, and it keeps growing. Reports from 2024 and 2025 say so, and a 2019 inspection found good canopy and sound growth. Other old oaks stand on the Oval and are probably survivors too. This is the one with the rings.
trees.access: Free. Open campus at Michigan State University in East Lansing, beside a public sidewalk.
trees.transport: On the MSU campus in East Lansing, about 5 km east of downtown Lansing; bus routes not checked.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the hollow trunk right beside the sidewalk, what is left of a white oak that was topped long ago. It stands on the Campus Oval near Beaumont Tower, among other old oaks, stop 8 on the campus tree tour.

trees.name: The Dawn Redwood of Beal Garden

location.address: W.J. Beal Botanical Garden, W Circle Dr, Michigan State University, East Lansing, MI 48824
location.neighbourhood: Michigan State University campus, East Lansing

trees.story:
Lightning has hit this tree hard enough that it now wears its own arrestor. Beal Botanical Garden in East Lansing planted this dawn redwood in 1954, sent from the Arnold Arboretum at a moment when the species was a botanical sensation. Dawn redwood had been thought extinct until living trees were found in China in the 1940s, and it was still new to collections when Michigan State University's garden got this one.

It has not led a quiet life since. Lightning struck in the 1990s and the top was taken off. A lightning arrestor went on in October 2012. Then in November 2017 the university announced that more than 20 feet would have to come off the top again, because of decay from the old lightning crack. A headline from 2025 reported it still standing.

The campus tree inventory holds a slightly different planting date, about 1953, against the garden's 1954. A state register lists a dawn redwood of 147.6 inches round at this garden in 2019, probably this one, though nobody has said so outright. It is the first stop on the campus tree tour, and at some seventy years old it is a young tree with a long medical history.
trees.access: Free. The W.J. Beal Botanical Garden is on the Michigan State University campus in East Lansing and open to visitors; check the garden's site for hours.
trees.transport: On the MSU campus in East Lansing, about 5 km east of downtown Lansing; bus routes not checked.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in winter, when this conifer stands bare. It is stop 1 on the campus tree tour, in Beal Botanical Garden; a state register places a dawn redwood just east of the stairway off W Circle Drive.
